content: The dew point is the temperature to which a specific parcel of air must be cooled, at a constant barometric pressure, for the water vapor within it to condense into liquid water. This condensed water is referred to as dew. The dew point represents the saturation point of the air. If the dew point temperature drops below freezing, it is often referred to as the frost point, as the water vapor no longer forms liquid dew but instead transitions directly into frost or hoarfrost through deposition. The dew point is closely related to relative humidity. A high relative humidity indicates that the dew point is near the current air temperature. When the relative humidity reaches 100%, the dew point equals the air temperature. If the dew point remains constant and the air temperature increases, the relative humidity will decrease. At a given barometric pressure, regardless of temperature, the dew point reflects the mole fraction of water vapor in the air, which determines the specific humidity of the air. The dew point is a critical parameter for general aviation pilots, as it is used to assess the likelihood of carburetor icing and fog formation, as well as to estimate the height of the cloud base. The behavior of water vapor in the air is independent of the presence of other gases. Dew formation occurs at the dew point even if the only gas present is water vapor. The dew point is a monotonic function of the partial pressure of water vapor, meaning it can be determined solely from the partial pressure of water vapor, and vice versa. At a constant barometric pressure, the dew point indicates the mole fraction of water vapor in the air, which determines the specific humidity. If the barometric pressure increases without altering the mole fraction, the dew point will rise, causing water to condense at a higher temperature. Conversely, reducing the mole fraction of water vapor will lower the dew point back to its original value. Similarly, increasing the mole fraction after a pressure drop will restore the dew point to its initial level. For example, the same dew point in New York and Denver (at a much higher altitude) implies a higher fraction of water vapor in the air in Denver compared to New York. At a constant temperature, the dew point reflects the absolute humidity of the air, independent of barometric pressure. If the temperature rises without changing the absolute humidity, the dew point will also rise, and water will condense at a higher pressure. Reducing the absolute humidity will lower the dew point back to its original value. Similarly, increasing the absolute humidity after a temperature drop will restore the dew point to its initial level. For instance, if the dew point and temperature are the same in New York and Denver, the mass of water vapor per cubic meter of air will also be the same in both cities. Humans often experience discomfort at high dew points. A high dew point corresponds to either a high ambient temperature, which causes the body to perspire and produce sweat, or a high relative humidity, which inhibits the evaporation of sweat and impairs the body’s ability to cool itself. This can lead to overheating and discomfort. Conversely, a lower dew point corresponds to a lower ambient temperature or lower relative humidity, both of which allow the body to regulate its temperature more effectively and avoid overheating. People accustomed to continental climates may begin to feel uncomfortable when the dew point reaches 15–20°C (59–68°F), and dew points above 21°C (70°F) are often considered oppressive. To calculate the dew point (Td) given the relative humidity (RH) and the actual air temperature (T), a commonly used approximation is: [ T_d = frac{b cdot gamma(T, RH)}{a gamma(T, RH)} ] where: [ gamma(T, RH) = frac{a cdot T}{b + T} + lnleft(frac{RH}{100}right) ] In this formula, temperatures are in degrees Celsius, and ln refers to the natural logarithm. The constants (a) and (b) are derived from the Magnus approximation for the saturation vapor pressure of water in air as a function of temperature. This approximation is considered valid within specific temperature ranges. A simpler approximation for converting between the dew point, dry bulb temperature, and relative humidity is: [ T_d = T frac{(100 RH)}{5} ] This rule of thumb is accurate to within ±1°C as long as the relative humidity is above 50%. For every 1°C difference between the dew point and the dry bulb temperature, the relative humidity decreases by approximately 5%, starting with RH = 100% when the dew point equals the dry bulb temperature. For example, if the relative humidity is 100%, the dew point equals the air temperature. At 90% relative humidity, the dew point is approximately 3°F lower than the air temperature. For every 10% decrease in relative humidity, the dew point drops by about 3°F.
